mainTopic: The laws of קריעה (tearing for a death): mending, size, location, adding onto a tear, special cases, and the mourner's meal
overview: This amud is mostly about קריעה, tearing one's garment for a death. It first explains which sewing counts as real mending (only the fine 'Alexandrian' kind) and which stitched spots on a garment a valid tear may be made over. It then covers whether a torn garment may be turned over and mended, and teaches that a buyer is bound by the same ban on mending as the seller. Next it records how long the first tear and an added tear must be, and עולא rules on that. It explains which part of a shared tear may be mended when a father and a son die one after the other. רבי יהודה בן בתירה requires a separate tear for parents, and שמואל rules like him, because קריעה is separate from אבילות. The amud then teaches how far down a tear may go and where to tear once the garment is full. A disagreement follows over whether a second death needs a new tear within seven days or within thirty days, and רבי זירא challenges both views. After more rules about borrowed cloaks, sick relatives, children and in-laws, the amud turns to the mourner's meal on upright or overturned beds, with a story about רבא. It ends by opening a ברייתא about a traveler, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The mending being discussed is Alexandrian mending
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא closes the previous point by saying that the mending in question is the high-quality 'Alexandrian' kind of sewing.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is talking about Alexandrian mending.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the discussion just before this section. It says the mending being talked about is the special, very fine 'Alexandrian' sewing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Not all sewing is the same. Ordinary rough stitching still leaves the tear easy to see, but Alexandrian mending is so fine that the tear basically disappears. By saying this, the גמרא limits the earlier rule to that strong kind of mending.

keyTerms.meaning: Mending, a careful sewing-up of a tear so the garment is whole again
Alexandrian, a very fine style of sewing from Alexandria that hides the tear

phrases.english: And [this refers] to Alexandrian mending.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּבְאִיחוּי אֲלֶכְּסַנְדְּרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the previous discussion on the daf by defining what kind of mending is meant.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The mending discussed is the fine Alexandrian kind, which makes the tear practically invisible.

steps.title: Tearing over stitched spots: when it counts and when it doesn't
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that tearing over loose stitches, hems, gathers or ladder-stitches does not count as a proper קריעה, but tearing over a mended spot does.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: If someone tears over loose basting, over a hem, over a gathered part, or over ladder-like stitches, he has not done his duty. If he tears over a mended spot, he has done his duty.
steps.whatsHappening: A ברייתא lists places on a garment where tearing for a mourner does NOT count, and one place where it DOES count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Loose stitches, hems, gathers and ladder-stitches are not really solid fabric, so tearing there is like tearing nothing, and he has not torn his garment. But a spot that was properly mended is treated as whole cloth, so tearing there counts. The idea is that a קריעה must be a real tear in a whole garment.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The Rabbis taught', the opening for a ברייתא
One who tears his garment (for mourning)
The hem or fringe edge of a garment
A gathered or pleated part of the garment
Did not fulfill / did fulfill his obligation

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One who tears over loosely tacked stitches,
over the hem, over the gathered part,
over the ladder-like stitches, has not fulfilled [his obligation].
phrases.notes: 'סוּלָּמוֹת' literally means ladders. These are stitches that look like the rungs of a ladder.

phrases.english: Over a mended spot, he has fulfilled [it].

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַקּוֹרֵעַ מִתּוֹךְ הַשְּׁלָל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a new ברייתא on a related topic: where on a garment a mourning tear counts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Tearing over weak or loose stitching does not count. Tearing over a properly mended spot counts.

steps.title: רב חסדא: only Alexandrian mending counts as whole
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא limits the ברייתא: the 'mended spot' where tearing counts must be mended in the fine Alexandrian way.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: And this too is talking about Alexandrian mending.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא explains the last line of the ברייתא. The 'mended spot' that counts is only one sewn with Alexandrian mending.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא said tearing over a mended spot counts. רב חסדא narrows this: only a spot mended so finely that the garment really looks whole counts. A spot with ordinary sewing would be like the weak stitches in the first list.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who adds a limiting explanation here

steps.confusionAlert: These are the same words as step 1, but here they are used for a new purpose. Step 1 is about which mending is meant earlier on the daf. Here רב חסדא is explaining which mended spot is good enough to tear over.

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said:
And [this refers] to Alexandrian mending.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: וּבְאִיחוּי אֲלֶכְּסַנְדְּרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the last clause of the ברייתא in step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Tearing over a mended spot counts only if it was mended in the fine Alexandrian way.

steps.title: One may turn the garment upside down and mend it
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא allows a person to turn the torn garment upside down and then mend the tear.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: He may turn it downward and mend it.
steps.whatsHappening: A new ברייתא gives a way to deal with a torn garment: turn it upside down and then mend it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Some mourning tears may not be properly mended. This ברייתא, as stated by the first opinion, permits turning the garment so the torn edge is at the bottom and then mending it. The next step brings someone who disagrees.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: One is permitted to turn it
upside down and mend it.
phrases.notes: 'It' is the garment with the mourning tear at its upper edge.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: רַשַּׁאי לְהוֹפְכוֹ לְמַטָּה וּלְאַחוֹתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ברייתא about mending a torn garment.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: First opinion: one may turn the torn garment upside down and mend it.

steps.title: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר forbids mending even after turning it
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר disagrees and forbids mending the garment even if it is turned upside down.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר forbids mending it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר argues with the first opinion of the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion allowed mending once the garment is turned around. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר holds that turning the garment does not help, and the ban on mending stays in place.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא who disagrees with the first opinion

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹסֵר לְאַחוֹתוֹ,
phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar forbids mending it,

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹסֵר לְאַחוֹתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the first opinion in step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even when the garment is turned upside down, mending is forbidden.

steps.title: The buyer may not mend it either, so the seller must tell him
steps.stepSummary: The ban on mending passes to a buyer of the torn garment, so the seller must inform the buyer.
steps.simpleTranslation: Just as the seller may not mend it, the buyer also may not mend it. So the seller must let the buyer know.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds that the ban on mending does not end when the garment is sold. The buyer is bound by it too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think the ban is personal to the mourner, so a new owner could mend it freely. The ברייתא says no: the ban stays with the garment itself. Since the buyer cannot know this by himself, the seller has a duty to tell him the tear is a mourning tear.
steps.whatToRemember: A mourning tear that may not be mended stays forbidden to mend even after the garment is sold, so the seller must tell the buyer.

phrases.english: and just as the seller is forbidden to mend it,
so too the buyer is forbidden to mend it.
And therefore the seller must
inform the buyer.
phrases.notes: He has to tell the buyer that the tear was made for mourning.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּכְשֵׁם שֶׁהַמּוֹכֵר אָסוּר לְאַחוֹתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with a further rule about selling the garment.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The buyer is bound by the ban on mending just like the seller, so the seller must inform him.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the ban on mending is tied to the garment, not only to the person who tore it.

steps.title: רבי מאיר: a first tear of a טפח, an addition of three fingers
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא records רבי מאיר's measures: the first tear must be a טפח long, and an added tear must be three fingerbreadths.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: The first tearing is a handbreadth, and the addition is three fingerbreadths. These are the words of רבי מאיר.
steps.whatsHappening: A new ברייתא asks how long a mourning tear must be. It opens with רבי מאיר's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two measures. One is for the first tear. The other is for an 'addition', when a person must tear again for another relative and lengthens the same tear. רבי מאיר requires a full טפח for the first tear and three fingerbreadths for each addition.

keyTerms.meaning: An addition, lengthening an existing tear

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: The initial tear is a handbreadth,
and the addition is three fingerbreadths,
phrases.notes: The 'addition' is when he must tear for another relative and simply lengthens the tear he already has.

phrases.english: these are the words of Rabbi Meir.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: תְּחִילַּת קְרִיעָה — טֶפַח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ברייתא on a new topic: the length of the tear.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר: the first tear is a טפח, and each addition is three fingerbreadths.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: a first tear of three fingers, an addition of any amount
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה requires only three fingerbreadths for the first tear, and any amount at all for an addition.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: The first tearing is three fingerbreadths, and the addition is any amount.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה disagrees with רבי מאיר and gives smaller measures.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each of רבי מאיר's measures is lowered by one level. The first tear needs only three fingerbreadths, which is רבי מאיר's measure for an addition. The addition has no minimum at all.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא who disagrees with רבי מאיר
Any amount at all, no minimum

steps.whatToRemember: רבי מאיר requires a טפח, then three fingers. רבי יהודה requires three fingers, then any amount.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
The initial tear is three fingerbreadths,
and the addition is any amount.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: תְּחִילַּת קְרִיעָה — שָׁלֹשׁ אֶצְבָּעוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רבי מאיר's measures in step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה: the first tear is three fingerbreadths, and an addition can be any size.

steps.title: עולא rules on the size of the first tear and of an added tear
steps.stepSummary: עולא decides the dispute from steps 7-8. For the first tear, the הלכה follows רבי מאיר. For an addition, the הלכה follows רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא said: The הלכה follows רבי מאיר about the first tear, and follows רבי יהודה about adding on.
steps.whatsHappening: עולא gives the final ruling on the argument between רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה. He takes one side from each of them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר said the first tear is a טפח and an addition is three fingerbreadths. רבי יהודה said the first tear is three fingerbreadths and an addition can be any amount. עולא combines them: the first tear is a טפח (like רבי מאיר), and an addition can be any amount (like רבי יהודה).

keyTerms.meaning: The practical law follows the opinion of...
The mourner's tearing of his garment
An addition, meaning lengthening an existing tear for a new death

steps.confusionAlert: עולא is not following one תנא all the way. He splits the ruling: רבי מאיר for the first tear, and רבי יהודה for the addition.

phrases.english: Ulla said:
The halacha follows Rabbi Meir regarding the tearing,
and the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda regarding the addition.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר עוּלָּא: הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר בִּקְרִיעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the dispute presented in steps 7-8
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The first tear must be a טפח long, and an addition can be any length.

steps.title: A teaching of רבי יוסי supports עולא's split ruling
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא in which רבי יוסי says exactly what עולא ruled: the first tear is a טפח, and an addition can be any amount.
steps.simpleTranslation: This was also taught in a ברייתא: רבי יוסי says, the first tear is a טפח, and the addition can be any amount.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that עולא's combined ruling is not new. A תנא, רבי יוסי, already held this exact view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might think it is odd to mix two opinions. The ברייתא shows that רבי יוסי held this combination as a single opinion of his own. So עולא is really following a known תנא.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also taught this way (a ברייתא supports the statement)
A handbreadth, about four fingers wide
Any amount at all, even tiny

phrases.english: It was also taught this way:
Rabbi Yosei says:
The first tearing is a handbreadth,
and the addition is any amount.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא נָמֵי הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports עולא's ruling in step 9
steps.raayaObject: עולא's ruling: first tear a טפח, addition any amount

steps.title: Father died first, then son: the father's part may never be mended
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא: a man tore for his father and then lengthened the same tear for his son. The lower part (the son's) may be mended. The upper part (the father's) may not.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: If they told him his father died and he tore, and then that his son died and he added to the tear, the lower part may be mended, but the upper part may not be mended.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new ברייתא about one tear that serves two different deaths. Each part of the tear keeps the rules of the person it was made for.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The tear started at the top for the father, so the upper part belongs to him. The extension below it was made for the son. A tear for a parent may never be properly mended, but a tear for other relatives may be. So only the son's lower section can be sewn up.

keyTerms.meaning: May be mended, meaning sewn back together properly
The lower part / the upper part of the tear
And he added on, lengthening the existing tear

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
They told him his father died, and he tore;
then that his son died, and he added on,
the lower part may be mended,
the upper part may not be mended.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אָמְרוּ לוֹ מֵת אָבִיו וְקָרַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new ברייתא about a single tear that serves two deaths
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a combined tear, the father's upper part may not be mended, but the son's lower part may be mended.

steps.title: Son died first, then father: the rule flips
steps.stepSummary: The reverse case: a man tore for his son and then lengthened the tear for his father. Now the upper part (the son's) may be mended, and the lower part (the father's) may not.
steps.simpleTranslation: If his son died and he tore, and then his father died and he added to the tear, the upper part may be mended, but the lower part may not be mended.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with the opposite order of deaths. It shows that the rule depends on whose tear each section is, not on whether it is on top or bottom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time the original upper tear was for the son, so it may be mended. The extension below was for the father, so it may never be mended. Comparing this with step 11 shows that each section follows the relative it was torn for.
steps.whatToRemember: In a single tear made for two deaths, each section keeps its own rule. The part torn for a parent can never be mended, wherever it is on the garment.

phrases.english: If his son died, and he tore;
then his father died, and he added on,
the upper part may be mended,
the lower part may not be mended.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵת בְּנוֹ וְקָרַע, מֵת אָבִיו וְהוֹסִיף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The mirror case of step 11, with the order of deaths reversed
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the son's tear is on top and the father's extension is below, only the upper part may be mended.

steps.title: News of several deaths at once: one tear for all
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: if he hears at one time that his father, mother, brother and sister died, he makes one tear for all of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: If his father, mother, brother and sister died, he makes one tear for all of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא moves to a new case, where several deaths are reported together. The first opinion (תנא קמא) says one tear covers everyone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In steps 11-12 the news came one death after another, so he added onto the tear. Here everything is heard at once. The תנא קמא holds that a single tear is enough even when parents are included.

phrases.english: If his father died, his mother died,
his brother died, and his sister died,
he tears one tear for all of them.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵת אָבִיו, מֵת אִמּוֹ, מֵת אָחִיו, מֵתָה אֲחוֹתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא with a new case where several deaths are heard at once
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the תנא קמא, one tear covers all relatives who died together, parents included.

steps.title: רבי יהודה בן בתירה: parents need their own separate tear
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה בן בתירה argues that the other relatives share one tear, but the father and mother get a separate tear, because nothing may be added onto a parent's tear.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה בן בתירה says: For all of them he makes one tear, and for his father and mother he makes one tear, because we do not add onto the tear for one's father and mother.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה בן בתירה disagrees with the תנא קמא from step 13. He requires a separate tear for parents.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His reason is that a parent's tear must stand on its own, and other relatives cannot be added onto it. Because of this, the other relatives' tear and the parents' tear must be two different tears. The תנא קמא allowed one tear for everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא who disagrees with the first opinion here
We do not add on (to an existing tear)

steps.confusionAlert: "קרע אחד" appears twice in his statement. It does not mean the same single tear. It means one tear for the other relatives and another, separate tear for the parents.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says:
For all of them, one tear,
and for his father and mother, one tear,
because we do not add on
to the tear for his father and mother.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתִירָה אוֹמֵר: עַל כּוּלָּן קֶרַע אֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the תנא קמא of step 13
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Parents require a separate tear, because nothing may be added onto a parent's tear.

steps.title: Why can't you add onto a parent's tear?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind רבי יהודה בן בתירה's view that a parent gets a separate tear.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רבי יהודה בן בתירה says nothing may be added onto a parent's tear. This short question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 14, רבי יהודה בן בתירה said the other relatives can share one tear, but the father and mother need their own. The גמרא now wants to know what makes a parent's tear different.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
phrases.notes: He means: why does רבי יהודה בן בתירה say a parent's tear can't be added onto (Step 14)?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind Step 14.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason a parent's tear may not be shared with or added onto.

steps.title: Because a parent's tear is not subject to additions
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק explains that a parent's tear does not take additions.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: Because they are not subject to addition.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק answers the question: a parent's tear belongs to a category that is not "added onto."
steps.deeperAnalysis: Other relatives' tears can be lengthened for a new death, as we saw with עולא's rule and the ברייתא of רבי יוסי. A parent's tear stands alone. One way to understand this is that a person has only one father and one mother, so this tear is never part of a chain of additions.

keyTerms.meaning: An addition, meaning lengthening an existing tear for a new death

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said:
Because they are not subject to addition.
phrases.notes: Literally, "they are not in addition." "They" means the tears for a father and mother.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A parent's tear is not something that additions are made onto.

steps.title: שמואל rules like רבי יהודה בן בתירה
steps.stepSummary: שמואל rules that the הלכה follows רבי יהודה בן בתירה.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: The הלכה follows רבי יהודה בן בתירה.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל gives a practical ruling: we follow רבי יהודה בן בתירה, so a parent always gets a separate tear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This settles the argument from Steps 13 and 14 in favor of רבי יהודה בן בתירה. That is the stricter opinion, because it requires an extra tear.

keyTerms.meaning: The practical law follows the view of...

phrases.english: Shmuel said:
The halakha is in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתִירָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the argument between the ברייתא's first opinion and רבי יהודה בן בתירה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The הלכה follows רבי יהודה בן בתירה: a parent's tear is separate.

steps.title: Doesn't שמואל always follow the lenient view in mourning?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges שמואל from his own rule that in mourning we follow the lenient opinion.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did שמואל really say this? But שמואל said: The הלכה follows the lenient opinion in mourning!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a contradiction. שמואל has a general rule to follow the lenient view in mourning, yet here he followed the strict view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה בן בתירה is stricter, because he requires a second tear. If שמואל always rules leniently in matters of אבל, why does he rule strictly here?

keyTerms.meaning: And did he really say this? (opens a challenge)

phrases.english: And did Shmuel really say this?
But didn't Shmuel say:
The halakha follows the words of the lenient one in mourning!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל הָכִי? וְהָאָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks שמואל's ruling in Step 17.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's ruling like רבי יהודה בן בתירה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שמואל's general rule is to follow the lenient view in mourning, but here he follows the stricter view.

steps.title: Mourning and tearing are separate areas
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that שמואל's lenient rule covers אבילות, not קריעה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Mourning is one thing, and tearing is another.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction: שמואל's rule to be lenient applies only to the laws of mourning, not to the laws of tearing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: קריעה is treated as its own area of law, separate from אבילות. So ruling strictly about tearing does not clash with being lenient about mourning.

keyTerms.meaning: Tearing one's garment for a death

phrases.english: Mourning is separate, and rending is separate.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבֵילוּת לְחוּד, קְרִיעָה לְחוּד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 18.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שמואל's lenient rule covers every law connected to a death, including tearing.
steps.terutzMaskana: The lenient rule covers only אבילות. קריעה is a separate area, so שמואל can rule strictly there.
steps.whatToRemember: שמואל rules like רבי יהודה בן בתירה, so a parent gets a separate tear. His "follow the lenient view" rule applies to אבילות, not to קריעה.

steps.title: How far may the tear go?
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that one may keep lengthening a tear down to the navel, and some say only to the heart.
steps.simpleTranslation: Until where may one tear? Until his navel. Some say: until his heart.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching about the limit for lengthening a tear when one keeps adding for more relatives. There are two opinions: to the navel, or to the heart.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This continues the topic of adding onto a tear (Steps 10 to 12). The first opinion allows the tear to go down to the navel. The יש אומרים give a shorter limit: the heart.

phrases.english: Until where does he rend?
Until his navel.
And some say: until his heart.

steps.triggerLanguage: עַד הֵיכָן קוֹרֵעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new detail about adding onto tears: the limit.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A tear may be lengthened down to the navel. Some say only to the heart.

steps.title: A hint from the פסוק: "rend your hearts"
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא brings a hint (not a full proof) for the "heart" limit from יואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even though there is no proof for this, there is a hint, as it says: "And rend your hearts and not your garments."
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא supports the opinion that the limit is the heart with a hint from a פסוק. It says clearly that this is only a hint, not a real proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק speaks of tearing "your hearts," which connects tearing to the heart. That links nicely to the "until the heart" limit. Calling it a זכר לדבר means the law does not truly come from this פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: A real proof for the matter
A hint or reminder for the matter, weaker than a proof
As it is said (introduces a פסוק)

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין רְאָיָה לְדָבָר,
phrases.english: Even though there is no proof for the matter,
there is a hint for the matter, as it is stated:
"And rend your hearts, and not your garments."

steps.triggerLanguage: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין רְאָיָה לְדָבָר, זֵכֶר לַדָּבָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the "until his heart" opinion of Step 20.
steps.raayaObject: The opinion that the tear goes until the heart
steps.confusionAlert: This is not a real proof. The ברייתא itself says "there is no proof," only a hint (זֵכֶר לַדָּבָר).

steps.title: What to do when the limit is reached or the garment is full
steps.stepSummary: Once the tear reaches the navel, he moves three fingers away and tears again. If the front is full he uses the back, and if the top is full he turns the garment over.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he reached his navel, he moves three fingerbreadths away and tears. If the front is full, he turns it to the back. If the top is full, he turns the bottom up.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives practical steps for someone who keeps getting more deaths: where to make the next tear once the old one has reached the limit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He may not keep lengthening past the navel. Instead he starts a new tear three fingerbreadths away. When there is no more room in front, he uses the back. When the top is used up, he turns the garment so the old bottom becomes the top, since a tear must be made at the top.

phrases.english: If he reached his navel,
he moves three fingerbreadths away and rends.
If it became full in front, he turns it to the back.
If it became full above, he turns it over from below.
phrases.notes: He flips the garment so the old bottom edge is now at the top, and tears there.

steps.triggerLanguage: הִגִּיעַ לְטִיבּוּרוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains what to do once the limit from Step 20 is reached.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Past the navel, start a new tear three fingerbreadths away. If the front is full use the back, and if the top is full turn the garment over.

steps.title: A tear at the bottom or sides does not count, except for a כהן גדול
steps.stepSummary: Tearing at the bottom or the sides of a garment does not fulfill the obligation, but a כהן גדול tears at the bottom.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who tears at the bottom or at the sides has not fulfilled his obligation. But a כהן גדול tears at the bottom.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes by saying where a tear does not count: at the bottom or on the sides. The one exception is the כהן גדול, who tears at the bottom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This explains why Step 22 had him flip the garment: a valid tear must be at the top. The כהן גדול is an exception. He is not allowed to tear his clothes in the normal way, so he makes his tear at the bottom.

keyTerms.meaning: He has not fulfilled his obligation
Tears (used here for the כהן גדול's tear)

phrases.english: And one who rends from below or from the sides
has not fulfilled his obligation.
Except that a High Priest tears from below.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַקּוֹרֵעַ מִלְּמַטָּה וּמִן הַצְּדָדִין לֹא יָצָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the rules of where to tear and adds the exception for the כהן גדול.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A tear must be at the top. A tear at the bottom or the sides does not count, except for a כהן גדול, who tears at the bottom.
steps.whatToRemember: The tear goes at the top of the garment, down to the navel (some say the heart). After that you start a new tear three fingers away, use the back, or flip the garment. Bottom or side tears don't count, except for a כהן גדול.

steps.title: New tear or added tear: seven days versus thirty days
steps.stepSummary: רב מתנה and מר עוקבא disagree. One holds that within seven days of the first death a mourner makes a new tear for a second death, and after that he adds to the old one. The other holds the cut-off is thirty days.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מתנה and מר עוקבא disagreed about this, and both quoted אבוה דשמואל and לוי. One said: during the whole seven days he makes a new tear, and after seven days he adds to the old one. The other said: during the whole thirty days he makes a new tear, and after thirty days he adds to the old one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a disagreement about a mourner who hears that another relative died while he is still mourning. Does he tear a fresh place, or just lengthen the tear he already has?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both opinions agree that early in the mourning a fresh tear is needed and later he may simply lengthen the old one. They only argue about where the line falls: seven days or thirty days.

keyTerms.meaning: He adds to the existing tear by lengthening it
The first seven days of mourning
The first thirty days of mourning

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the whole discussion that follows. רבי זירא will try to find the reasoning behind each time limit and then challenge it.

phrases.aramaic: פְּלִיגוּ בַּהּ רַב מַתְנָה וּמָר עוּקְבָא,
phrases.english: Rav Mattana and Mar Ukva disagreed about it,
phrases.notes: "It" is a mourner who hears about a second death while he is still mourning the first.

phrases.english: and both said it in the name of Shmuel's father and Levi.
One said: all seven days, he tears anew;
after seven days, he adds to the first tear.
And one said: all thirty days, he tears anew;
after thirty days, he adds to the first tear.

steps.triggerLanguage: פְּלִיגוּ בַּהּ רַב מַתְנָה וּמָר עוּקְבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the rules about how to tear, the גמרא now asks when a second death needs a separate tear.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Within a set period (seven days or thirty days, depending on the opinion), a second death needs a new tear. After that period, he only lengthens the old tear.

steps.title: רבי זירא challenges the seven-day view from a woman's tear
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא suggests the reason for the seven-day view: during the seven days the tear may not be basted, so it still counts as an open tear. But a woman may baste her tear right away. Would she then be allowed to just add to it?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא objected: According to the one who says he makes a new tear all seven days, why is that? Because he may not baste the tear during the seven days. But then, what about what the Master said, that a woman may baste her tear immediately? Here too, should she be allowed to just add to it?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא first guesses the reason behind the seven-day opinion. Then he attacks that reason using the rule about a woman.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the seven-day rule depends on the tear still being open, then a woman, who may baste hers at once, should be allowed to simply add to it even during the seven days. That sounds wrong, so the suggested reason seems weak.

keyTerms.meaning: To baste it, a loose, temporary stitching of the tear

steps.confusionAlert: שולל means loose, temporary stitching. It is not a full, proper repair. That is a different word, איחוי, which comes in the next challenge.

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira strongly objected to this:

phrases.aramaic: מַאן דְּאָמַר כׇּל שִׁבְעָה קוֹרֵעַ, אַמַּאי —
phrases.english: The one who says he tears anew all seven days, why?
Because he is not permitted to baste it.
phrases.notes: Since the tear stays open all seven days, adding to it would just look like part of the first tear.

phrases.english: But then, what about that which the Master said:
a woman may baste it immediately,
would it be so here too?!
phrases.notes: He means: would a woman then be allowed just to add to her old tear during the seven days?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַבִּי זֵירָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This attacks the reasoning behind the first opinion in step 24.
steps.kashyaTarget: The seven-day opinion, along with its suggested reason that the tear may not be basted.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the rule depends on not basting, then a woman, who may baste right away, should be allowed to add to her old tear. That would be an odd result.

steps.title: A woman's basting is only for her dignity
steps.stepSummary: The woman's permission to baste is only out of respect for her. As far as the law is concerned, her tear still counts as open.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, it is because of the woman's dignity.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers רבי זירא's challenge to the seven-day view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A woman may baste early only so she is not left exposed. That is a special allowance for dignity, and it does not mean her tear is considered closed. So her tear still counts as open, and she too must make a new tear within seven days.

phrases.english: There, it is because of the woman's dignity.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This answers the challenge in step 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes the cases: the woman's rule is a special allowance and not a sign that her tear is closed.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A woman's early basting shows that her tear no longer counts as open.
steps.terutzMaskana: Her basting is allowed only for dignity, so her tear still counts as open, and the seven-day reason still holds.
steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם מִשּׁוּם כְּבוֹד אִשָּׁה הוּא

steps.title: רבי זירא challenges the thirty-day view from a parent's tear
steps.stepSummary: The suggested reason for the thirty-day view is that the tear may not be properly mended during thirty days. But a tear for a father or mother may never be mended. Would that mean he can never add to it and must always make a new tear?
steps.simpleTranslation: According to the one who says he makes a new tear all thirty days, why is that? Because he may not properly mend it during that time. But then, for his father and mother, whose tear may never be mended, would it be the same, so that he must always make a new tear?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא now does the same thing to the second opinion. He guesses its reason and then challenges it. The next step answers this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the thirty-day rule depends on the tear not yet being properly mended, then a parent's tear, which can never be mended, would mean a new tear is needed forever. That seems too extreme, so the reason looks questionable.

keyTerms.meaning: To properly mend it, a full repair
For his father and his mother

phrases.aramaic: מַאן דְּאָמַר כׇּל שְׁלֹשִׁים קוֹרֵעַ, אַמַּאי —
phrases.english: The one who says he tears anew all thirty days, why?
Because he is not permitted to properly mend it.
But then, for his father and his mother,
where he is never permitted to properly mend it,
would it be so too?!
phrases.notes: He means: would he then have to make a brand-new tear forever, and never just add to it?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאן דְּאָמַר כׇּל שְׁלֹשִׁים קוֹרֵעַ, אַמַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending the seven-day view, רבי זירא turns to challenge the thirty-day view.
steps.kashyaTarget: The thirty-day opinion, along with its suggested reason that the tear may not be properly mended.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A parent's tear may never be mended, so by this reason a new tear would be needed forever, which is an extreme result.

steps.title: The father-and-mother tear stays open only out of honor
steps.stepSummary: A tear for a parent may never be mended, but that is only to honor the parent. Legally, after thirty days it counts as if it were sewn up, so for a new death he may simply add to it.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, it is only because of the honor of his father and mother.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 27. Never mending a tear for a parent is about honor, not about the tear legally staying 'open.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question was this: if the thirty-day view rests on 'the tear may not be mended,' then a parent's tear, which is never mended, should need a brand-new tear forever and never be added onto. The answer separates the practice from the legal status. Not mending is a sign of respect, but after thirty days the tear is treated as if it were sewn, so he may add onto it. This answer has the same shape as the answer about the woman in Step 26.

keyTerms.meaning: There, in that case (the tear for a father or mother)
The honor owed to one's father and mother

steps.whatToRemember: Both the seven-day view and the thirty-day view survive their challenges. Special rules (a woman basting her tear, never mending a parent's tear) are about honor and do not change whether the tear legally counts as open.

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם מִשּׁוּם כְּבוֹד אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ הוּא.
phrases.english: There, it is because of the honor of his father and mother.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם מִשּׁוּם כְּבוֹד אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 27
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes a respect-based practice from the legal status
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since a parent's tear is never mended, it stays legally open forever, so for any later death he must always make a new tear and may never add onto it.
steps.terutzMaskana: Not mending is only for honor. Legally, after thirty days the tear counts as if mended, so for a new death he may add onto it (מוֹסִיף), just like any other tear after thirty days.

steps.title: Wearing an old tear before the dead is deception
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that someone who walks before a מת in a garment torn earlier for a different death 'steals' from the dead and from the living.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: One who goes out before the dead person in a torn garment steals from the dead and from the living.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא. Wearing a garment already torn for someone else when walking before a מת is forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He 'steals' from the dead person because he never actually tore for him. He 'steals' from the living because onlookers think he tore in this person's honor, so he is fooling them. This fits the earlier discussion, where a new death usually needs a real tear of its own.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One who goes out in a torn garment before the dead person

phrases.aramaic: הֲרֵי זֶה גּוֹזֵל אֶת הַמֵּתִים וְאֶת הַחַיִּים.
phrases.english: steals from the dead and from the living.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן הַיּוֹצֵא בְּבֶגֶד קָרוּעַ לִפְנֵי הַמֵּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New ברייתא on the topic of קריעה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Wearing a previously torn garment before a מת, as if one had torn for him, is forbidden deception of both the dead and the living.

steps.title: Tearing a borrowed cloak when one's father dies
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: if someone borrowed a cloak saying he was visiting his sick father, and the father had died, he may tear it, mend it, return it, and pay for the damage. If he never mentioned the visit, he may not touch it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: If a person says to his friend, 'Lend me your cloak so I can go visit my father, who is sick,' and he goes and finds that his father has died, he tears it and mends it. When he gets home, he returns the cloak and pays for the tear. But if he did not tell him, he may not touch it.
steps.whatsHappening: A ruling about tearing a cloak that belongs to someone else. Whether it is allowed depends on whether the owner knew where the borrower was going.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner knew the father was sick, he lent the cloak knowing it might need to be torn. So tearing is allowed, as long as the borrower pays for the loss in value. Without that information the owner never agreed, so tearing his cloak is forbidden. The borrower may also mend the tear properly, since it is not his own garment to keep torn.

keyTerms.meaning: The value lost because of the tear

steps.confusionAlert: Paying 'the value of the tear' does not mean buying the whole cloak. He returns the cloak and pays only for the drop in its value.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
One who says to his friend: Lend me your cloak

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵלֵךְ וַאֲבַקֵּר אֶת אַבָּא שֶׁהוּא חוֹלֶה,
phrases.english: and I will go and visit Father, who is sick,
and he went and found that he had died,
he tears it and mends it,
and when he comes home, he returns his cloak to him,
and gives him the value of the tear.
But if he did not inform him,
he may not touch it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר הָאוֹמֵר לַחֲבֵירוֹ הַשְׁאִילֵנִי חֲלוּקְךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with another case about a garment in mourning
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A borrower who told the owner he was visiting his sick father may tear the cloak for the father's death, then mend it, return it, and pay for the damage. Without telling him, he may not tear it.

steps.title: Shielding a sick person from news of a death
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: when a sick person's relative dies, we do not tell him, we do not tear clothing in front of him, and we quiet the women crying near him.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: If a relative of a sick person dies, we do not tell him, in case he becomes too upset. We do not tear in front of him, and we quiet the women in his presence.
steps.whatsHappening: A new ברייתא about a sick person whose relative has died. Everyone hides the death from him to protect his health.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The concern is that the shock and grief could overwhelm him and make his illness worse. So besides not telling him directly, people avoid the outward signs of mourning around him: tearing clothes and the women's crying.

keyTerms.meaning: His mind will become overwhelmed or unsettled

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that protecting a sick person's health comes before the usual public signs of mourning.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A sick person who had a relative die:
we do not inform him that he died,
in case he loses control of his mind.
And we do not tear in front of him,
and we quiet the women in his presence.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן חוֹלֶה שֶׁמֵּת לוֹ מֵת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New ברייתא on a related mourning topic
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A sick person is not told of a relative's death, and tearing and wailing are kept away from him, so that he will not be overwhelmed.

steps.title: Tearing for a child and for in-laws
steps.stepSummary: We tear a child's garment to stir up grief, and a man tears for his father-in-law or mother-in-law out of respect for his wife.
steps.simpleTranslation: We tear the clothing of a small child to stir up sadness. And a man tears for his father-in-law and mother-in-law, out of respect for his wife.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with two more cases where we tear clothing even though it is not strictly required.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קטן has no duty of קריעה, but tearing his clothing makes everyone feel the loss more deeply. A man does not formally mourn his in-laws, but he tears anyway to show his wife that he shares her mourning.

keyTerms.meaning: A minor, a child who is not yet obligated in מצוות
Sadness and grief of the heart

phrases.english: And we tear the garment of a minor
because of the grief it arouses.
And one tears for his father-in-law and for his mother-in-law,
because of the honor of his wife.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמְקָרְעִין לַקָּטָן מִפְּנֵי עׇגְמַת נֶפֶשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא's list of קריעה rules
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A child's garment is torn to arouse grief, and a man tears for his in-laws to honor his wife.

steps.title: A mourner should not hold a small child on his lap
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא quotes אבל רבתי: a mourner should not hold a child on his lap, because the child may make him laugh and people will think badly of him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: It was taught in אבל רבתי: A mourner should not put a small child on his lap, because the child will make him laugh, and people will look down on him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא adds another rule about mourners, this one about how a mourner should behave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Holding a child is not forbidden in itself. The worry is that playing with the child will make the mourner laugh, and laughing during mourning looks disrespectful to people who see it.

keyTerms.meaning: A collection of teachings about mourning (also called שמחות)
He becomes disgraced in people's eyes

phrases.english: And רב פפא said,
It was taught in אבל רבתי:

phrases.aramaic: אָבֵל לֹא יַנִּיחַ תִּינוֹק בְּתוֹךְ חֵיקוֹ,
phrases.english: A mourner should not place a child in his lap,
because it brings him to laughter,
and he ends up disgraced in the eyes of people.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב פָּפָּא, תָּנָא בְּאֵבֶל רַבָּתִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a related teaching about a mourner's behavior
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A mourner should not hold a child on his lap, because it may lead to laughter and disgrace.

steps.title: Upright or overturned beds at the mourner's meal
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about serving the meal on upright beds. A ברייתא explains that a close friend eats with the mourner on overturned beds, while anyone else eats on upright beds.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said the mourner's meal is served on upright beds. The Rabbis taught: If someone goes to a mourner's house and is very close with him, they serve them on overturned beds. If not, they serve them on upright beds.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to a new line in the משנה and brings a ברייתא that explains when the beds stay upright.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Mourners usually sit on overturned beds. If the visitor is a close friend, he can join the mourner fully, so the beds stay overturned. If the visitor is not that close, the beds are set upright so that he is not made to sit like a mourner.

keyTerms.meaning: Serving the mourner's first meal after the burial (סעודת הבראה)
Upright beds, set the normal way
Overturned beds, the usual sign of mourning
He is very familiar and close with him

steps.confusionAlert: Upright beds here do not mean the mourner stops mourning. It is a courtesy so that a visitor who is not a close friend does not have to sit like a mourner.

phrases.english: And the meal is served only on upright beds.
The Rabbis taught:
One who goes to the house of the mourner,
if he was very familiar with him
— they serve him the meal on overturned beds.
And if not
— they serve him the meal on upright beds.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין מַבְרִין עַל מִטּוֹת זְקוּפוֹת. תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new line of the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A close friend eats with the mourner on overturned beds, while a less close visitor eats on upright beds.

steps.title: רבא and a visitor who acted too familiar
steps.stepSummary: When רבא was mourning, אבא בר מרתא visited. רבא set the bed upright, but אבא בר מרתא turned it over. רבא said this young scholar had no sense.
steps.simpleTranslation: Something bad happened to רבא, and אבא בר מרתא (who is אבא בר מניומי) came to visit him. רבא set the bed upright, and אבא בר מרתא turned it over. רבא said: How little sense this young Torah scholar has!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that shows the ברייתא's rule about beds in real life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By setting the bed upright, רבא was signaling that he did not count the visitor as a close friend. אבא בר מרתא ignored that signal and turned the bed over as if he were very close, so רבא criticized his lack of sense.

keyTerms.meaning: Something bad happened to him, a polite way of saying a relative died

steps.whatToRemember: How the beds are set at the mourner's meal depends on how close the visitor really is. The mourner decides, and a visitor should not claim more closeness than he has.

phrases.english: Something bad happened to רבא,
phrases.notes: This is a gentle way of saying someone close to him died.

phrases.english: אבא בר מרתא came in to him,
who is אבא בר מניומי.
רבא set the bed upright,
אבא בר מרתא turned it over.
He said: How little sense there is
in this young Torah scholar.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אִיתְּרַע בֵּיהּ מִילְּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A story that shows the ברייתא's rule about upright and overturned beds
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A visitor should not act as a close friend when the mourner has signaled that he is not one.

steps.title: A new teaching about someone who is traveling
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins quoting a ברייתא about a person traveling from one place to another. The ruling itself has not been given yet.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught in a ברייתא: someone who is going from one place to another place...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is opening a new ברייתא and introducing a case about a traveler. This line only sets up the case; the rule comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 31 through 35 dealt with how a mourner behaves and how others act around him. Now the גמרא turns to a new situation: a mourner who is on the road. We only hear who the case is about; what he must do has not been said yet.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The רבנן taught.' This phrase introduces a ברייתא, a teaching from the time of the משנה that was not included in the משנה.
Someone who is going or traveling
From one place to another place

steps.confusionAlert: Do not look for the ruling in this line. It is only the opening of the case, and the rule comes next.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One who goes from place to place

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַהוֹלֵךְ מִמָּקוֹם לְמָקוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the story of רבא and אבא בר מרתא in step 35 to a new ברייתא about a mourner who is traveling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling yet. This line only introduces a case about a person traveling from place to place.
